title: Ordinary Differential Equations
subject: Differential Equations
summary: First-order methods, linear second-order equations with constant coefficients (oscillators, damping, resonance), Laplace transforms and impulse response, linear systems via eigenvalues, phase portraits and linearisation, series solutions, and numerical methods. Built on MIT 18.03 lectures and Boas ch. 8, with the chemist's rate equations, damped vibrations and oscillating reactions as recurring examples.

units.title: First-Order Equations
units.summary: Separable and linear first-order ODEs, direction fields, autonomous equations and stability: the mathematics of first-order kinetics and relaxation.

lessons.title: ODEs, Direction Fields and Separable Equations
objectives: Classify an ODE by order, linearity and homogeneity, and state what a general solution and an initial-value problem are.
Sketch a direction field for y' = f(x, y) and use it to predict the qualitative shape of solutions.
Solve separable equations including rate laws dc/dt = -k c^n, and give the integral solution for n = 0, 1, 2.
Check a proposed solution by substitution and determine the constant from initial data.
Connect to chemistry: derive the integrated rate laws for zero-, first- and second-order reactions and half-lives.

objectives: Solve y' + p(x) y = q(x) with an integrating factor and verify the result.

Use substitutions (homogeneous equations, Bernoulli equations) to reduce an equation to a solvable form.
Decide when an equation is exact and solve it via a potential function (connecting to conservative fields).
Connect to chemistry: solve consecutive reactions A -> B -> C and a CSTR/mixing-tank problem with an integrating factor.

lessons.title: Autonomous Equations, Stability and Euler's Method
objectives: Find equilibria of y' = f(y) and classify each as stable or unstable from the sign of f'(y*).
Draw and interpret a phase line, including semi-stable points, and explain why solutions cannot cross equilibria.
Apply Euler's method by hand for a few steps and state its local and global error orders.
Explain how a step size that is too large produces spurious behaviour (instability) for y' = -ky.

units.title: Second-Order Linear Equations: Oscillators and Resonance
units.summary: The harmonic oscillator in all its guises: free, damped, driven and resonant. Applies directly to molecular vibrations, RLC circuits and driven spectroscopic transitions.

lessons.title: Homogeneous Equations and the Characteristic Equation
objectives: Solve a y'' + b y' + c y = 0 by the characteristic equation for real distinct, repeated and complex roots.
State why solutions form a two-dimensional vector space and define the Wronskian as the independence test.
Write the oscillatory solution in the form e^{-gamma t}(A cos(w t) + B sin(w t)) = R e^{-gamma t} cos(wt - phi).
Fit constants to initial position and velocity.

objectives: Classify damping as under-, critical or over-damped from the discriminant and the damping ratio zeta.
Compute the damped frequency, decay time and quality factor Q for an underdamped oscillator.
Sketch x(t) for each damping regime, and say which returns to equilibrium fastest.
Model an RLC circuit and a spring-mass-dashpot with the same equation and map the parameters.
Connect to chemistry: a vibrational mode with friction/relaxation gives a Lorentzian line shape; Q is related to linewidth.

Use the exponential-response formula y_p = e^{st}/P(s) and handle the exceptional case P(s) = 0 by multiplying by t.
Apply variation of parameters when undetermined coefficients fail.

units.title: Laplace Transforms, Impulses and Convolution
units.summary: The Laplace transform turns linear constant-coefficient ODEs into algebra and gives the response to steps and impulses (delta functions), the engine behind Green's functions.

Derive L{f'} = sF - f(0) and use it to turn an ODE into an algebraic equation.
Invert transforms with partial fractions and a table.
Solve a damped, driven oscillator IVP by Laplace transform and identify transient and steady-state terms from the poles.

units.title: Linear Systems and Phase Portraits
units.summary: Systems du/dt = Au solved by eigenvalues, classified by the trace and determinant, and extended with the matrix exponential; coupled oscillators and kinetics.

lessons.title: First-Order Systems and the Eigenvalue Method
objectives: Convert an n-th order ODE and a pair of coupled ODEs into a first-order system u' = A u.
Solve u' = A u for distinct real eigenvalues as u = c1 e^{l1 t} v1 + c2 e^{l2 t} v2 and fit initial data.
Interpret the solution as normal modes of a coupled two-mass-spring system.
Use the superposition principle for homogeneous systems and the Wronskian/fundamental-matrix idea.

units.title: Nonlinear Systems and Stability
units.summary: Linearisation near equilibria, stability, limit cycles and chaos: predator-prey, the pendulum and oscillating chemical reactions.

objectives: Find the critical points of a 2D autonomous system and compute the Jacobian at each.
Classify each critical point from the eigenvalues of the Jacobian and state when linearisation is inconclusive (centres, degenerate cases).
Sketch the global phase portrait using nullclines and the local portraits, for example for Lotka-Volterra and for a damped pendulum.
Find a conserved quantity or Lyapunov function to establish stability when linearisation fails.

Describe a Hopf bifurcation as the birth of a limit cycle when a complex pair crosses the imaginary axis.
Explain sustained oscillation in the Brusselator or Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction as a limit cycle, and name the feature (autocatalysis) required.

units.title: Series Solutions and Special Equations
units.summary: Power-series and Frobenius solutions of linear ODEs with variable coefficients: the source of Legendre and Bessel functions (used heavily in M5, hydrogen atom, and the harmonic oscillator in QM).

Solve Cauchy-Euler (equidimensional) equations x^2 y'' + a x y' + b y = 0 via y = x^r.
Use the Wronskian and Abel's formula to test independence without solving.
Explain why the radial equation in 3D problems often takes Cauchy-Euler form.

objectives: Solve y'' + p y' + q y = 0 about an ordinary point by substituting y = sum a_n x^n and deriving the recurrence relation.
State the radius of convergence of the series solution from the nearest singularity.
Derive Legendre's equation from the Laplacian in spherical coordinates and obtain the polynomial solutions P_l for integer l.
Obtain Hermite polynomials from the series solution of the quantum harmonic oscillator equation and see how termination quantises the energy.

lessons.title: Regular Singular Points, Frobenius Method and Bessel's Equation
objectives: Identify a regular singular point and write the indicial equation.
Carry out the Frobenius method y = x^r sum a_n x^n to find at least one solution, and state when a logarithm appears in the second.
Derive the Bessel function J_nu(x) from Bessel's equation and sketch J_0, J_1.
Explain the role of Bessel functions in cylindrical problems (vibrating drum, waveguide), previewing M5.
Connect to chemistry: the radial hydrogen equation is a Frobenius problem giving the Laguerre polynomials and the quantised energies.

units.title: Numerical Methods for ODEs
units.summary: How computers integrate ODEs: Euler, midpoint, Runge-Kutta, error, stability and stiffness; the tools you will use in later simulations.

Explain stiffness using a fast-decaying plus slow mode (chemical kinetics with disparate rate constants) and why implicit methods help.
Choose a method for a given task, including when energy-conserving (symplectic) methods are preferred, as for planetary orbits.
